title: US Founding Documents
author: Continental Congress, Constitutional Convention and US Congress
openingText: When, in the course of human events, one people must dissolve the political bonds tying them to another and take their separate, equal place among the world's powers — the place to which the Laws of Nature and of Nature's God entitle them — a basic respect for the opinions of humankind requires that they declare the reasons that compel them to separate.
about:
This collection contains the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution as drafted in 1787, the first ten amendments known as the Bill of Rights, and Amendments XI–XXVII. The Articles of Confederation are not included.

The Declaration argues for separation from Britain through claims about rights, consent and resistance to tyranny. The Constitution sets out the powers and limits of Congress, the presidency and the courts, and the relationship between the federal government and the states. The amendments change that framework, from protections for individual rights to the abolition of slavery and changes to elections and presidential succession.

Reading note: the original constitutional provisions remain in their historical form, even where later amendments change them. Read the later amendments alongside the original clauses; this collection is not a consolidated statement of current law. Slavery-related provisions and the Declaration's derogatory description of Indigenous peoples are retained as part of the historical documents, not endorsed. The modern editions clarify the language without removing these contradictions. Distinctive American legal terms, including grand jury, probable cause and equity, retain their historical meaning.

whyItMatters.title: Rights and their limits
whyItMatters.body: The Declaration's claim that all people are created equal sits beside the Constitution's provisions accommodating slavery. Read these tensions alongside the Thirteenth, Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments.

whyItMatters.title: Who may exercise power?
whyItMatters.body: The Constitution distributes authority among institutions and states. Its rules about elections, appointments, vetoes and impeachment make those relationships concrete.

whyItMatters.title: A document that can change
whyItMatters.body: The amendment process allows later generations to alter the original framework. Compare the original presidential election rules with the Twelfth Amendment, or the selection of senators with the Seventeenth.

angleCards.title: Follow the Declaration's argument
angleCards.text: Trace the movement from rights and consent to grievances and the announcement of independence.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how the Declaration's grievances support its argument for independence.

angleCards.title: Follow a power through the Constitution
angleCards.text: Choose taxation, lawmaking or appointments and track who proposes, approves and checks each action.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand how the Constitution distributes and limits specific powers.

angleCards.title: Read original clauses with their amendments
angleCards.text: Compare the original election and slavery-related provisions with the later amendments that change them.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare the original Constitution with later amendments without treating superseded provisions as current law.
